STEEL
J.A.

INTRODUCTION

1

These two appeals raise the issue of the proper balance between
the constitutional right to freedom of expression and the need to regulate the
conduct of members of the legal profession.

BACKGROUND

2

These appeals arise from the same proceeding before a panel of
the Discipline Committee of The Law Society of Manitoba.  Mr. Histed, a lawyer
and member of The Law Society of Manitoba, was found to have breached the
Code
of Professional Conduct
(the
Code
) by sending a letter dated January
14, 2004, to opposing counsel that commented on a number of judges by stating:

[Justice A], frankly, is a bigot.  [Justice B], although fair,
intelligent, and a really nice guy, would not move the matter forward on a
timely basis. [Justice C] is not familiar enough with civil proceedings and is
too right wing.  [Justice D] is too right wing.

3

Histed was retained by clients engaged in residential school
litigation involving, among others, the Attorney General of Canada.  In the
context of that litigation, Histed and opposing counsel were to agree to a
consensual list of three judges from which the Associate Chief Justice of the
Court of Queen’s Bench was to select a case management judge.  It was in the
context of a series of letters between counsel attempting to agree on that list
of three judges that the letter in question was written by Histed.

4

In that letter, Histed rejected names put forward by counsel from
the federal Department of Justice, Aboriginal Law Services Department,
representing the Attorney General, and made the comments mentioned

above.  A copy of the letter was also sent to counsel for the two co‑defendants
in the litigation.

5

The lawyer who received the letter, in turn, forwarded it to a
senior lawyer in her department.  That lawyer sent a copy to the Law Society.  The
Law Society authorized charges of professional misconduct and a citation issued
against Mr. Histed alleging:

… [Y]ou failed in your duties owed to other lawyers, the courts, the
profession and the public by writing a letter which was offensive and otherwise
inconsistent with the proper tone of a professional communication, and in which
you inappropriately criticized the judiciary contrary to Chapters 1, 9, 13, 15
and 19 of the
Code of Professional Conduct
.

6

An inquiry into the charge was held before a panel of the
Discipline Committee, and Histed was found in breach of the
Code
with
respect to his comments calling Justice A “a bigot,” but not with respect to
the comments concerning the other three judges mentioned in the letter.

7

In his appeal, as well as in front of the panel, Histed argues
that the letter was stated to be on a “Strictly Confidential and Without
Prejudice” basis and therefore should not have been received in evidence by the
panel.  To do so was a violation of
The
Privacy Act
, R.S.M. 1987, c.
P125, or, alternatively, a violation of the principle of settlement privilege.
He further argues that the opinion expressed in his letter was protected by the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
(the
Charter
), and
therefore the
Code
and/or the panel’s decision violated his right to
freedom of expression.

8

Following the finding of the panel, and prior to the sentencing
portion of the disciplinary proceeding against him, Histed brought an
application in the Court of Queen’s Bench seeking an order prohibiting the Law
Society from proceeding to sentencing.  The motions judge denied the
application, indicating that a multiplicity of proceedings should be avoided
and that there was an adequate alternative remedy available by way of appeal to
the Court of Appeal under
s. 76
of
The
Legal Profession Act
, S.M. 2002,
c. 44 – Cap. L107 (the
Act
).

9

In a separate appeal, Histed appeals that decision of the motions
judge, arguing that the judge erred when he dismissed his application for a
prohibition order.  He alleges that the judge failed to consider
Charter

values, as well as other relevant factors, and failed to provide adequate
reasons for his decision.

10

There is no appeal as to the reasonableness of the finding of the
panel or the sentence imposed of a fine of $2,500 and costs of $7,500.

THE STATUTORY FRAMEWORK

11

The
Act
and the Law Society Rules, enacted pursuant to the

Act
, comprise a comprehensive scheme under which the legal profession in
Manitoba regulates itself through its governing body, the Law Society.  As
articulated in the
Act
, the purpose of the Law Society is to “uphold and
protect the public interest in the delivery of legal services with competence,
integrity and independence” (s. 3(1)).  In furtherance of that mandate, s. 3(2)
details that the Law Society must:

(a)       establish standards for the education, professional
responsibility and competence of persons practising or seeking the right to
practise law in
Manitoba
; and

(b)       regulate the practice of law in
Manitoba
.

12

The
Code
was promulgated pursuant to s. 43(b) of the
Act
,
which states that the benchers may “establish or adopt a code of conduct for
lawyers and students.”  The
Code
does not form part of the rules, but is
a separate and distinct document which was adopted by the benchers of the Law
Society in 1992.  The preface of the
Code
contains the following
observation:

With few exceptions the statutes do not specify the kinds of conduct
that will subject a lawyer to discipline.  For its part, the Code does not
attempt to define professional misconduct or conduct unbecoming, nor does it
try to evaluate the relative importance of the various rules or the gravity of
a breach of any of them.  By enunciating principles of what is and is not
acceptable professional conduct, the Code is designed to assist governing
bodies and practitioners alike in determining whether in a given case the
conduct is acceptable, thus furthering the process of self-government.

13

The panel accepted the Law Society’s position that the charge
against Histed was to be considered with reference to several chapters of the
Code

which should be read together in determining whether Histed failed to meet an
acceptable standard of practice in his letter.  This included Chapters 1, 9, 13
(particularly at Commentary 4), 15 and 19.  The relevant portions of the
chapters are attached to these reasons as an appendix.

14

Section 76(1) of the
Act
allows for appeals to the Court
of Appeal.

STANDARD OF REVIEW

15

I do not believe it is necessary to review the pragmatic and
functional test in detail in this decision.  In this particular case, the
question of the admissibility of the letter presents itself as a pure question
of law.  The application of the
Charter
to the facts before the panel is
also a question of law that is not within the specific expertise of the panel.
As such, both issues attract a standard of correctness.  On the other hand, the
panel’s findings on the facts as to whether Histed’s conduct contravened the
provisions of the
Code
and thereby constituted professional misconduct are
factual findings within the specific expertise of the panel and therefore
attract a standard of reasonableness
simpliciter
.  See
Histed v. Law
Society of
Manitoba
,
2006 MBCA 89
, 208 Man.R. (2d) 44.

PROHIBITION APPLICATION – DOCKET NO.
AI06-30-06547

16

This appeal may be dealt with briefly.  It is moot.  Histed was
already sentenced by the panel on November 14, 2006.

17

Nonetheless, Histed argues that the motions judge erred in the
exercise of his discretion because he failed to consider
Charter
values,
relevant factors and failed to give reasons when exercising his discretion.  It
is also submitted that the statutory remedy will not be adequate in these
circumstances and therefore the court should exercise its discretion to hear
the appeal notwithstanding its mootness.  See
Borowski v.
Canada

(Attorney General)
,
1989 CanLII 123 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 342.

18

The requirement of reasons must be given a functional and
purposeful interpretation.  See
R. v. Sheppard
,
2002 SCC 26
, [2002] 1
S.C.R. 869.  The reasons of the motions judge are not elaborate, but they are
sufficient in the context of these proceedings and provide the basis for a
meaningful review by this court.

19

Avoiding an unnecessary multiplicity of proceedings is a basic
principle of justice which all courts attempt to follow when appropriate and
when there are no circumstances that would demand otherwise.  This court has on
several occasions confirmed that courts ought to be slow to intervene in the
administrative process when that process provides for an appeal within the administrative
scheme.  See
Mondesir v.
Manitoba
Association of Optometrists

(1998),
1998 CanLII 19440 (MB CA)
, 129 Man.R. (2d) 96 (C.A.), leave to appeal to S.C.C. refused, [1998]
S.C.C.A. No. 405 (QL), which comments were recently quoted with approval by
Hamilton J.A. in
Histed
, at para. 53.

20

There are no exceptional circumstances that were presented that
would have led the motions judge to decide differently.  In a case relied on by
Histed,
Adelaar v. Law Society of British Columbia
,
2000 BCSC 329
(in
chambers), the court did order a judicial stay of the proceedings before the
respondent or, alternatively, an order of prohibition.  However, in that case,
the remedy was based on the finding that the Law Society’s 34-month delay in
the proceedings amounted to a breach of the administrative principles of
natural justice and fairness, as well as a breach of the principles of
fundamental justice.  These are not the facts in our case.

21

Here, the statute provides an adequate remedy of an appeal to
this court, which could be invoked in the ordinary course once the
administrative tribunal has completed its work.  That is exactly the nature of
the other appeal filed by Histed in this case.  It is in that other appeal that
the court will consider
Charter
values and whether the panel’s decision
conforms to the constitutional requirements of the
Charter
.  Moreover,
this court has the power to provide an adequate remedy under
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter
,
should it be necessary.

22

It is argued further that Histed’s prohibition application was
wider than simply prohibiting the Law Society from continuing the proceeding.
Histed applied to the Court of Queen’s Bench for:

(1)

an order prohibiting and enjoining the Law Society from commencing or
proceeding with any disciplinary action against Histed for the expression of a
political opinion;

(2)

an order that the Law Society apologize to Histed for the infringement
and denial of his fundamental freedom of expression; and

(3)

an order that the Law Society develop and implement a corporate
compliance program designed to ensure that the Law Society complies with the
Charter

in the future.

23

Thus, Histed argued at the hearing that even though his
application to prohibit the Law Society from proceeding to the sentencing
portion of the hearing may be moot, his motion requesting other items was still
in play.  He cited no authorities in support of this argument.  Again, the
remedy requested would require a determination of the constitutionality of the
panel’s decision, something that is already under appeal in this court.

24

To have the issue adjudicated at the Court of Queen’s Bench level
while the proceedings in front of the tribunal were not yet completed would
have given Histed another “kick at the cat.”  The resulting effect would be to
encourage and endorse a multiplicity of hearings for no good reason.  Instead,
I agree with the motions judge that the administrative process should have been
allowed to run its course.

25

So, not only is the matter moot, but it is not the type of issue
that this court should exercise its discretion to hear notwithstanding the fact
that it is moot.

26

The appeal with respect to the motions judge’s order to deny
Histed’s request for a prohibition order is dismissed.

ADMISSIBILITY OF LETTER – DOCKET NO.
AI06-30-06548

Impact of
The Privacy Act

27

Histed alleges that the letter was obtained by the Law Society in
violation of his privacy.  He notes that s. 7 of
The Privacy Act

provides:

Effect on law of evidence

7
No
evidence obtained by virtue or in consequence of a violation of privacy in
respect of which an action may be brought under this Act is admissible in any
civil proceedings.

As a result, Histed argues that the
letter should not have been considered as evidence before the Law Society.

28

I do not believe
The Privacy Act
has any application to
this case.  The letter was in the hands of the Law Society with the consent of
the letter’s recipient, counsel for the Attorney General.  Section 3(d) of
The
Privacy Act
states that it is only a violation of a person’s privacy to use
“his letters … without his consent or without the consent of any other person
who is in possession of them with his consent.”

29

This letter was authored, signed and distributed by Histed to
counsel for the Attorney General and copied to counsel for two co-defendants in
the litigation.  One of the recipients, who was in possession of the letter
with Histed’s consent, objected to its content, and the letter was forwarded
first to senior counsel within the department and then to the Law Society.
Given that the recipient was in possession of the letter with Histed’s consent,
it does not come within the parameters of
The Privacy Act
.  There was no
violation of Histed’s privacy rights, or those of his clients, that would
render the letter inadmissible under s. 7 of
The Privacy Act
.

30

That in itself is sufficient to dispose of the argument with
respect to the application of
The Privacy Act
.  Consequently, it is
unnecessary for me to deal with other issues, such as whether the disciplinary
proceeding is in the nature of a civil proceeding to which the
Act
would
apply or whether, even if a violation of privacy had occurred, it could be
argued that the Law Society had viable defences available to it pursuant to s.
5(c), (d) and (f)(i) of
The Privacy Act
.  See, for example,
Hung v.
Gardiner
,
2002 BCSC 1234
, 45 Admin. L.R. (3d) 243, aff’d
2003 BCCA 257
, 1
Admin. L.R. (4
th
) 152.

Settlement Privilege

31

Histed also argues that the letter was protected by settlement
privilege and therefore should not have been disclosed to the Law Society by
the department.  The Law Society acknowledges that settlement privilege is not
addressed by the
Act
, but argues that an analogy may be drawn to the
Act
’s
references to solicitor-client privilege in ss. 67, 77 and 82(1).  These
sections allow the Law Society to override solicitor-client privilege for the
purposes of performing its function of regulating the conduct of members of the
profession.

32

As summarized in John Sopinka, Sidney N. Lederman & Alan W.
Bryant,
The Law of Evidence in Canada
, 2d ed. (Toronto:  Butterworths
Canada Ltd., 1999) (at para. 14.207):

There are a number of conditions that must be present for the
[settlement] privilege to be recognized:

(a)

a litigious dispute must be in
existence or within contemplation;

(b)

the communication must be made
with the express or implied intention that it would not be disclosed to the
court in the event negotiations failed; and,

(c)

the purpose of the communication
must be to attempt to effect a settlement.

33

The fact that the phrase “Strictly Confidential and Without
Prejudice” was written at the top of the letter does not attach privilege to
the letter if, in fact, the letter was not sent as part of a settlement
negotiation.  The substance of the letter has to be considered.  The selection
of a case management judge was a procedural issue.  While the rules of the
Manitoba Court of Queen’s Bench do not specifically provide for a case
management procedure (with one exception not relevant to these reasons), a
practice has developed that it is not uncommon for counsel to request a case
management judge to be appointed.  I emphasize that the parties here
contemplated, as Histed acknowledged during his submissions before the panel, a
case management judge who would set dates, give directions, be available to
hear interlocutory motions and generally to move an action along.  This is
quite different than a judge who would conduct a judicial alternative dispute
resolution, a practice also common in the Manitoba Court of Queen’s Bench.  I
make no comment on the role of the latter with respect to the issue of
settlement privilege.  It is sufficient for our purposes to confirm that the
facts in this case support the finding that the parties contemplated the role
of this judge as one of case management and thus procedural only.  Therefore,
the purpose of this communication was not an attempt to effect a settlement.
As such, the panel held, and I agree, that settlement privilege does not attach
to this letter.

34

I also agree with the panel that even if the letter could be
considered to be a communication sent as a part of a settlement negotiation or
a first step toward that negotiation, nonetheless, the letter should have been
admitted as evidence.

35

This court discussed settlement privilege in the case of
Histed
v. Law Society of Manitoba
,
2005 MBCA 106
, 195 Man.R. (2d) 224 (in
chambers).  I stated (at para. 37):

The
protection afforded settlement communications is less stringent than that
afforded solicitor-client privilege.  It is not considered a substantive rule
of law or a fundamental civil right.  Consequently, a court will more likely
carry out a balancing of interests to determine whether the circumstances
justify a demand for production or, in our case, justify straying from the open
court policy.

36

Recently, in the case of
Meyers v. Dunphy
,
2007 NLCA 1
, 38
C.P.C. (6
th
) 265, the Newfoundland and Labrador Court of Appeal held
(at para. 27):

Where exclusion of the communication would facilitate an abuse of the
privilege, or another compelling or overriding interest of justice requires it,
without prejudice communications are admissible.

See also,
Rush & Tompkins Ltd.
v. Greater London Council
,
[1988] 3 All E.R. 737 at 740 (H.L.)
.

37

Solicitor-client privilege has often given way to the overriding
principle that members of the Law Society must be required to make full
disclosure of their activities as professionals when under investigation by the
Law Society in its disciplinary persona.  Not only have the courts confirmed
this principle (see
Robertson Stromberg, Re
(1995),
1995 CanLII 3909 (SK CA)
, 128 Sask.R. 107
(C.A.), and
Skogstad v. The Law Society of British Columbia
,
2007 BCCA
310
, [2007] 9 W.W.R. 218, at para.
8
), but the
Act
itself provides for
the need for accountability to take precedence over solicitor-client
privilege.  See ss. 67 and 77 of the
Act
.  It seems to me that the same
result should obtain, in most cases, in a balancing of interests between the
need to protect the public by allowing the Law Society the fullest opportunity
to investigate the conduct of their members and the desire to encourage
settlement.

38

I agree with the panel when it concluded that “there is a greater
public interest in the ethical practice of law than the public interest in
encouraging settlement negotiations by protecting those negotiations from
disclosure.”  In the situation at bar, where the disclosure does not compromise
the interests of any party in the process of the main litigation (such as
disclosing a settlement proposal might), but is extraneous to the main cause
and only exposes a potentially unprofessional communication from counsel which may
trigger a finding of professional misconduct, the panel’s comments seem
particularly apt.

DIVISION OF POWERS

39

Histed submitted that any necessary regulation of free political
speech falls within federal, not provincial, jurisdiction.  While acknowledging
that the regulation of the professions is a matter within provincial
competence, he argued that such regulatory authority should not be understood
to extend to the regulation of the free political speech of members of the
professions.

40

Assuming for the moment that referring to a judge as a bigot in
correspondence between counsel is “political” (as categorized by Histed in his
factum), the argument is still without merit.  Histed does not refer to a
particular head of federal jurisdiction upon which to base this argument.  I
presume he is referring to the federal government’s jurisdiction over criminal
law.  The pith and substance of the
Act
is to regulate the legal
profession and thereby protect the public interest.  There is a difference
between criminal laws which intrude upon freedom of speech, such as contempt or
hate speech, and the regulation of a certain level of conduct among the members
of the legal profession in relation to each other and the tribunals before
which they appear.

41

The case of
R. v. Kopyto
(1987),
1987 CanLII 176 (ON CA)
, 39 C.C.C. (3d) 1 (Ont. C.A.),
is a good example.  Although the court found the accused not guilty of criminal
contempt because of his comments, they agreed that he had acted in an
unprofessional manner which could attract the sanction of the Law Society.  In
fact, a case cited by Histed further supports this conclusion.  In
Krieger
v. Law Society of Alberta
,
2002 SCC 65
, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 372, Krieger was
charged with professional misconduct in the discharge of his duties as a
criminal prosecutor.  While the Supreme Court agreed that there were certain
decisions of Crown prosecutors that could not be reviewed by the Law Society,
they also agreed that other decisions may require review.  The court held (at
para. 4):

As a consequence of its exclusive jurisdiction over property and civil
rights in the province, under
s. 92(13)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
,
the Legislature of Alberta has the power to regulate the legal profession,
which it has duly conferred upon the Law Society under the
Legal Profession
Act
.  Because Crown prosecutors must be members of the Law Society, it
thereby follows Crown prosecutors are subject to the Law Society’s code of
professional conduct.  All conduct that is not protected by the doctrine of
prosecutorial discretion is subject to the conduct review process.

42

If Histed has a remedy, it lies in the
Charter
, not in the
division of powers.

CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND
FREEDOMS

43

Section 32
of the
Charter
limits its application to the
“government” and its actions.  The Law Society’s mandate under the
Act

is part of a regulatory scheme established by the Manitoba legislature to
govern the affairs and activities of the legal profession.  The
Charter

applies to the exercise of statutory authority regardless of whether the actor
is part of the government or is controlled by the government.  See cases such
as
Law Society of Manitoba v. Savino
(1983),
1983 CanLII 2995 (MB CA)
, 23 Man.R. (2d) 293 (C.A.),
Re
Klein and Law Society of Upper Canada
(1985),
1985 CanLII 3086 (ON HCJDC)
, 50 O.R. (2d) 118 (Div. Ct.),
and particularly,
Rocket v. Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario
,

1990 CanLII 121 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 232, where the Supreme Court of Canada confirmed that the
Charter

applied to professional regulatory bodies and limits they placed on freedom of
expression, albeit in the context of the dental profession.  See also,
Professor Peter W. Hogg,
Constitutional Law of Canada
, 5
th

ed., looseleaf (Toronto:  Carswell, 2007) vol. 2 at para. 37.2(c).  The
Charter

applies both to the provisions of the
Act
and to the decision of the
panel.  See
Slaight Communications Inc. v. Davidson
,
1989 CanLII 92 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R.
1038, and
Rocket
.

44

Histed argued that s. 43(b) of the
Act
, Chapters 1, 9, 13,
15 and 19 of the
Code
and the decision of the panel infringed his
freedom of expression guaranteed by
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

45

Little need be said of the importance of freedom of expression in
our legal system.  In fact, the Supreme Court has adopted an expansive approach
to
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
generally.  See, for example,
R. v. Butler
,

1992 CanLII 124 (SCC)
, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 452 at 488, and
Ross v.
New Brunswick

School District No. 15
,
1996 CanLII 237 (SCC)
, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 825.  Therefore, the breach of this

Charter
right is rightly conceded by the Law Society.

46

But, as with other rights and freedoms guaranteed by the
Charter
,
freedom of expression is not absolute.  There are situations in which the
freedom of one individual must be qualified so that other important social
values may be respected and protected.  These competing claims are reconciled
by requiring that any curtailment of expression be justified under s. 1 as a limit
that is reasonable in a free and democratic society.

47

Histed raises two main arguments with respect to the s. 1
justification in this case.  First, he argues that the provisions of the
Code

contain only vague statements of principle, admonitions, and advice which fail
the “prescribed by law” requirement of s. 1 and thus do not constitute
reasonable limits.  For example, there is no express prohibition against
criticism of the judiciary.  Second, he submits that the Law Society adduced no
evidence to satisfy its onus to prove on the balance of probabilities that the
Code

and its application in this case were reasonable limits.

Vagueness and Section 1 of the
Charter

– “Prescribed By Law”

48

Limits must be articulated with some precision or they cannot be
considered to be prescribed by law as required by the words of s. 1.  Law
cannot be vague, undefined or totally discretionary.

49

The courts apply a very high threshold when addressing vagueness
under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.  A thorough discussion of vagueness and its
relationship with the phrase “prescribed by law” was undertaken by Gonthier J.
on behalf of the Supreme Court in the case of
R. v. Nova Scotia
Pharmaceutical Society
,
1992 CanLII 72 (SCC)
, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 606.  Certain principles arose from
that decision.

50

To begin with, the vagueness doctrine does not require absolute
certainty.  Absolute precision in the law rarely exists, if at all.  The
question is whether the legislature has provided an intelligible standard by
which the judiciary may make a determination.  Moreover, the interpretive role
of the courts and the need for flexibility should not be overlooked.  It is
possible that several varying judicial interpretations of a given provision may
exist, but that does not mean the provision is vague.  See
Nova Scotia

Pharmaceutical Society
, at pp. 622-23, 626-27.

51

Specifically, Gonthier J. went on to discuss the
boundaries of the vagueness concept (at p. 639):

By setting out the boundaries of permissible and
non-permissible conduct, these norms give rise to legal debate.  They bear
substance, and they allow for a discussion as to their actualization. They
therefore limit enforcement discretion by introducing boundaries, and they also
sufficiently delineate an area of risk to allow for substantive notice to
citizens.

52

Fundamentally, the
Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society
case
summed up the vagueness doctrine in one question:  Does the provision so lack
precision that it does not give sufficient guidance for legal debate?  In other
words, can a court or tribunal reach a conclusion as to its meaning by reasoned
analysis applying legal criteria?

53

Pursuant to s. 43(b) of the
Act
, the
benchers of the Law Society are authorized to make and adopt codes of
professional conduct.  There were several provisions of the
Code
that
the panel held to be applicable to this case.  Taking all these provisions
together, I find that they provide guidance and an intelligible standard to the
panel, even though the panel may apply certain interpretive techniques to those
provisions and even though different panels may reach different conclusions.

54

For example, the
Code
provision (Chapter 15,
Commentary 3) reads as follows:

The lawyer should not in the course of a professional
practice write letters, whether to a client, another lawyer or any other
person, that are abusive, offensive or otherwise totally inconsistent with the
proper tone of a professional communication from a lawyer.

55

In my opinion, the use of the words “abusive,
offensive or otherwise totally inconsistent with the proper tone of a
professional communication from a lawyer” are the type of norms referred to by
Gonthier J. in
Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society
.  The decision
regarding which comments may ground charges of professional misconduct is
neither arbitrary nor is it left solely to the discretion of the Law Society.
Instead, it is bounded by these norms.  A conviction does not automatically
follow from the decision to prosecute.  See
Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical
Society
, at p. 636.

56

This is confirmed by the fact that Histed’s
references to other judges in the same letter were held not to contravene the
Code
.
Moreover, Histed has been charged with writing abusive or offensive letters in
previous Law Society proceedings.  See
Law Society of Manitoba v. Histed
,
[2003] L.S.D.D. No. 31 (QL).  In that case, the panel held that Histed’s choice
of words was ill-advised, intemperate and short of the standard of polite
discourse that one might otherwise expect, but that the communications fell
short of professional misconduct.

57

Moreover, the
Code
can be considered to be a
“law” for the purposes of s. 1.  There is clear statutory authority for the
adoption of this
Code
under s. 43(b) of the
Act
.  See
British
Columbia Public School Employers’ Assn. v. B.C.T.F.
,
2005 BCCA 393
, 257
D.L.R. (4
th
) 385 at para.
39ff
.  Additionally, McLachlin J. (as she
then was), in
Committee for the Commonwealth of Canada v. Canada
,
1991 CanLII 119 (SCC)
, [1991]
1 S.C.R. 139 at 245, observed that justification under s. 1 should not be
limited to legislation or regulations because such an approach would require
legislatures to enact regulations dealing with every contingency as a
pre-condition of a public body justifying its conduct.  Such a requirement, she
concluded, would not accord with the spirit of the
Charter
and would
make it unduly difficult for the government to justify reasonable or necessary
limits on rights.

Evidentiary Issues and
Section 1

58

The second argument raised by Histed relates to the
nature and the extent of the evidence presented by the Law Society to justify
the panel’s decision under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

59

In proving that the infringement under s. 2(b) is
justified, the onus is on the Law Society to prove on a balance of
probabilities that the infringement is reasonable and can be demonstrably
justified in a free and democratic society:

To this end, two requirements must be met.  First, the
legislative objective being pursued must be sufficiently important to warrant
limiting a constitutional right.  Next, the means chosen by the state authority
must be proportional to the objective in question:  ….

[
Multani v. Commission scolaire Marguerite-Bourgeoys
,
2006 SCC
6
,
[2006] 1 S.C.R. 256
, at para.
43
,
following
R. v. Oakes
,
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
,
[1986]
1 S.C.R. 103
, and
R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd.
,
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
,
[1986] 2 S.C.R.
713
]

60

There have been a number of cases which have confirmed the
importance of the objectives being considered here.  Those cases have confirmed
that the legislation and codes of professional conduct are directed toward two
important objectives; namely, the protection of the administration of justice
and the protection of the public.  Those objectives have been found to be
sufficiently pressing to warrant infringing freedom of expression.

61

In
Kopyto
, a lawyer was charged with criminal contempt of
court by scandalizing the court in uttering words about the judiciary and the
judicial system that were intended to bring a court into contempt or to lower
its authority.  While the Ontario Court of Appeal ultimately held that the
means chosen to regulate contempt of court were not reasonable or demonstrably
justified, they did agree that the objective of protecting the administration
of justice was of sufficient importance to warrant overriding the right to
freedom of expression (at p. 27,
per
Cory J.A. (as he then was)):

It was conceded by counsel for the intervenant and I am satisfied that
the first criterion was met in that the objective of protecting the
administration of justice was of sufficient importance to warrant overriding a
constitutionally protected right or freedom.

62

The second objective, the protection of the public, has also been
found by the Supreme Court of Canada to be an objective of sufficient
importance to justify an infringement of the right to freedom of expression.
In the case of
Rocket
, the Supreme Court acknowledged the importance
that regulation plays in maintaining a high standard of professionalism and
protecting the public (at p. 249):

It is difficult to overstate the importance in our society of the
proper regulation of our learned professions.  Indeed, it is not disputed that
the provinces have a legitimate interest in regulating professional
advertising.  The maintenance of professionalism and the protection of the
public are at the heart of such regulations.

63

While the
Rocket
case concerned the regulation of
advertising and its connection to the need to protect the public, its comments
on the need to maintain a high standard of professionalism and its link to
protection of the public is also relevant in this situation.

64

The public relies on the expertise of lawyers in a wide variety
of circumstances in which integrity and professionalism are key components.
Surely the public benefits by having all lawyers held to a high standard of
professionalism.

65

The case of
Pearlman v. Manitoba Law Society Judicial
Committee
,
1991 CanLII 26 (SCC)
, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 869, discusses the importance of an independent
legal profession to a free and democratic society, although not necessarily
within the strict confines of a s. 1 analysis.  The court quoted from a study
paper entitled
The Report of the Professional Organizations Committee

(Toronto:  Ministry of the Attorney General, 1980), which concluded that the
self-governing status of the professions, and of the legal profession in
particular, was created in the public interest.  The court quoted from p. 26 of
the report, where it stated (at p. 887):

Stress was rightly laid on the high value that free societies have
placed historically on an independent judiciary, free of political interference
and influence on its decisions, and an independent bar, free to represent
citizens without fear or favour in the protection of individual rights and
civil liberties against incursions from any source, including the state.

66

The Supreme Court agreed in the
Pearlman
case that the
general public has a vested interest in the ethical integrity of the legal
profession and such public interest requires a law society to enforce a code of
conduct by disciplining its members.  See pp. 889-90.

67

Next, the court must determine that the means chosen are
proportional to the objective.  The requirement of proportionality balances the
interests of the public in its protection and in the maintenance of the
administration of justice with an individual’s right to speak freely.  This
proportionality test has been held to consist of three components.  The
legislation and, in this case, the decision of the panel must have a rational
connection to the objectives.  So the measures adopted cannot be arbitrary or
unfair.  The means chosen must impair the constitutional right as little as is
reasonably possible and there must be proportionality between the effects of
the measures which are responsible for limiting the
Charter
right and
the objective.  See
Multani
, at para.
43
, and
R. v. Big M Drug Mart
Ltd. et al.
,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295.  In the application of these criteria,
the legislature is entitled to some deference in their choice of measures.

The impairment must be “minimal”, that is, the law must be carefully
tailored so that rights are impaired no more than necessary.  The tailoring
process seldom admits of perfection and the courts must accord some leeway to
the legislator.  If the law falls within a range of reasonable alternatives,
the courts will not find it overbroad merely because they can conceive of an
alternative which might better tailor objective to infringement:  ….

[
RJR-MacDonald Inc. v.
Canada
(Attorney General)
,
1995 CanLII 64 (SCC)
,
[1995] 3 S.C.R. 199
at para.
160]

68

In the
Kopyto
case, it is interesting to note that while
the Ontario Court of Appeal felt that criminalizing Kopyto’s conduct was not
demonstrably justifiable under
s. 1
of the
Charter
, the same was not
true of subjecting him to professional discipline.  Comments may be
unprofessional even if they do not amount to criminal contempt.  The court
stated (at p. 79,
per
Dubin J.A.):

… [A]lthough I find the appellant not guilty of the offence charged, he
is not free from any disciplinary action which the Law Society may choose to
institute against him.

69

Dubin J.A., in that same case, quoted from the United States
Supreme Court in the case of
In re Sawyer
, 79 S.Ct. 1376 at 1388 (1959),
where Justice Stewart stated (at p. 80):

If, as suggested by my Brother Frankfurter, there runs through the
principal opinion an intimation that a lawyer can invoke the constitutional
right of free speech to immunize himself from even-handed discipline for proven
unethical conduct, it is an intimation in which I do not join.  A lawyer
belongs to a profession with inherited standards of propriety and honor, which
experience has shown necessary in a calling dedicated to the accomplishment of
justice.  He who would follow that calling must conform to those standards.

Obedience to ethical precepts may require abstention from what in other
circumstances might be constitutionally protected speech.

70

The provisions of the
Code
set out certain guidelines.
Applying those guidelines to the case at hand, the decision was not arbitrary,
unfair or based on irrational considerations.  Lawyers are not absolutely
precluded from criticizing the judiciary.  In fact, “the courts, like other
public institutions, should be open to lively and trenchant criticism.”  See
Kopyto
,
at p. 11.

71

Not only should the judiciary be accountable and open to
criticism, but lawyers play a very unique role in ensuring that
accountability.  As professionals with special expertise and officers of the
court, lawyers are under a special responsibility to exercise fearlessness in
front of the courts.  They must advance their cases courageously, and this may
result in criticism of proceedings before or decisions by the judiciary.  The
lawyer, as an intimate part of the legal system, plays a pivotal role in
ensuring the accountability and transparency of the judiciary.  To play that
role effectively, he/she must feel free to act and speak without inhibition and
with courage when the circumstances demand it.  This is acknowledged and
encouraged by the
Code
.  See the
Code
, Chapter 9, Commentary 1.
As quoted by Justice Frankfurter in
Sawyer
(at p. 1399) and adopted by
the court in
Kopyto
(at p. 81):

We are a society governed by law, whose integrity it is the lawyer’s
special role to guard and champion.

[
In re Howell
,
89 A.2d 652
at 653 (N.J. Sup.
Ct.
1952)
(concurring opinion)
]

So, there is no question that lawyers
must have the right to speak truth to power.

72

On the other hand, as the cases have shown, there must be some
limits attached to that criticism where it would affect the administration of
justice or the protection of the public.  A fine balance must be achieved.

73

That is why the provisions of the
Code
focus on context.  As
the Supreme Court explained in the
Ross
case (at para.
78
):

… [T]he
Oakes
test
should be applied flexibly, so as to achieve
a proper balance between individual rights and community needs.  In undertaking
this task, courts must take into account both the nature of the infringed right
and the specific values the state relies on to justify the infringement.  This
involves a close attention to context.  McLachlin J. [as she then was] in
RJR-MacDonald
,

supra
, reiterated her statement
in
Rocket v. Royal College of Dental
Surgeons of Ontario
,
1990 CanLII 121 (SCC)
,
[1990] 2 S.C.R. 232
, at pp. 246-47
, that conflicting
values must be placed in their factual and social context when undertaking a s.
1 analysis.

74

Time, place and circumstances determine the constitutional
protection of speech.  The nature of the harm and the inability to measure it,
the vulnerability of the group protected, subjective fears and apprehension of
harm and the nature of the infringed activity must all be considered.  See
R.
v. Bryan
,
2007 SCC 12
, [2007] 1 S.C.R. 527, at para.
10
.

75

The judiciary should be open to criticism, but to operate
effectively, the legal system must operate with some degree of civility and
respect.  Criticism must be within certain parameters.  Lawyers are required by
the
Code
to avoid the use of abusive or offensive statements,
irresponsible allegations of partiality, criticisms that are petty or
intemperate and communications that are abusive, offensive or inconsistent with
the proper tone of a professional communication.

76

With respect to the rational connection between the objectives of
protecting the public and maintaining respect for the administration of justice
and the impugned provisions, the panel found, and I agree, that:

As stated earlier in these reasons, the criticism of Justice A strikes
at the very foundation of his role as a judge.  Any person believing Justice A
to be a bigot would feel justified in refusing to proceed in any proceeding for
which he was appointed.  Any person who believed Justice A to be a bigot would
rightly believe any prior proceeding before Justice A would be tainted.  After
all, Histed, a lawyer, a person in a position to know, has stated as a fact
that the judge is a bigot.  Unquestionably, the administration of justice
requires justice to be done and to be seen to be done.  Justice cannot be
dispensed by a bigot nor can it be seen to be done by a bigot.  There is a
clear rational connection between the objective of the Law Society and the
impugned provisions.

77

In relation to the question of minimal impairment, it is
important to note the restrictions placed on Histed relate to the manner of
expression.  He is free to express himself in other ways while still
representing his clients’ interests.  It was open to him to reject the names of
those judges put forward by opposing counsel without the use of the offensive
term that he used to attack the judge’s integrity.  However, his statement in a
professional communication directed to other lawyers that the named judge was a
bigot was offensive and unprofessional.  Had he believed in the truth of the
statement, it would have been appropriate to bring his complaint to the
attention of the Judicial Council.

78

In
B.C.G.E.U. v. British Columbia (Attorney General)
,

1988 CanLII 3 (SCC)
, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 214, the Supreme Court of Canada upheld an injunction
enjoining a union from striking in front of the court house on the basis that
it interfered with the administration of justice.  The court concluded that the
injunction impaired the union’s freedom of expression as little as possible because
it (at p. 248)

… left the Union and its members free to express themselves in other
places and in other ways so long as they did not interfere with the right of
access to the courts.

79

While litigants and other interested persons may comment publicly
on cases before the courts and may criticize judicial decisions in terms which
some might consider offensive, lawyers are bound by the constraints of the
professional standards which apply to all members of the legal profession.
Similar to Mr. Ross in the case of
Ross
, who was free to exercise his
fundamental freedoms in a manner unrestricted by the order, but only upon
leaving his teaching position, if Histed wishes to have that same unfettered
right to criticize the administration of justice, he may do so, but not while a
member of the Law Society.

80

Support for a finding that a limited prohibition on freedom of
expression within a regulated profession can be justified is found in the
Rocket

case.

81

The third factor to be considered is whether there is proportionality
between the restriction and the stated objectives.  Given the minimal
impairment, as already described, the limited value attached to insults as
forms of expression and the nature of the penalty imposed, it follows that the
negative effects on freedom of expression were not so deleterious as to
outweigh the benefit of protecting the administration of justice and regulating
the profession.

82

I find that the infringement is justified under s. 1.

83

One last issue must be addressed.  Histed argued in front of the
panel and on appeal that in order to satisfy its burden, the Law Society had to
adduce some evidence to establish that the administration of justice was or
could have been undermined by this letter.  I understand this point to relate
to two areas.  Histed has challenged both the provisions of the
Code
and
the decision of the panel itself.  So, the court must decide that both are a
reasonable limit under s. 1.  See
Slaight Communications
and
Rocket
.

84

As Professor Jamie Cameron found in her article, “Back to
Fundamentals:  Multidisciplinary Partnerships and Freedom of Association Under
Section 2(d) of the
Charter
” (2000), 50 U.T.L.J. 261,
Charter
claims in
respect of regulatory bodies, whether they be legal, medical or other, can
arise in one of two ways (at p. 266):

First, as the Court
found in
Rocket v. Royal College of Dental
Surgeons of Ontario
, legislation may be invalid on its face, as an
impermissible infringement of the
Charter
.  Second, legislation that is valid
on its face may be applied in a way that violates the Charter, since a body
exercising authority on behalf of, or as a delegate of, the state is bound by
the Charter as though it were government.

85

With respect to the issue of evidence under s. 1,
the panel held:

… [N]o further evidence was required to be led by the
Law Society to persuade us upon a preponderance of probabilities that limits in
the Code were demonstrably justified.  As has been stated in these reasons, it
is well recognized that a scurrilous attack on a judge undermines the
administration of justice.  The attack made by Histed was to the essential
fundamental quality of integrity that must exemplify the character of every
judge.

….  The administration of justice in this Province is
clearly undermined if the members of the judiciary includes, or is perceived to
include, bigots.

86

The nature of the evidence required to be adduced
to justify a s. 1 limit has been a controversial issue for many years in
Charter

jurisprudence.  In fact, most recently the central debate in many s. 1 cases is
the quality of the evidentiary record.  See, for example, the comments in Sujit
Choudhry, “So What Is the Real Legacy of
Oakes
?  Two Decades of
Proportionality Analysis under the Canadian
Charter
’s
Section 1
”
(2006),
34 S.C.L.R. (2d) 501
.

87

In
Oakes
, Dickson C.J.C. indicated that,
generally speaking, clear and cogent evidence should be adduced to justify a
Charter

breach.  However, he did indicate that “there may be cases where certain
elements of the s. 1 analysis are obvious or self-evident” (at p. 138).

88

It has not always been easy to determine which were
the “obvious or self-evident” cases.  What are the circumstances in which it is
appropriate to apply “logic” or “common sense” to surmount an absence or
insufficiency in evidence to justify the infringement of a
Charter

right?  Some academics have argued that:

The Court has yet to work out under what circumstances
it will use common sense, reason or logic to bridge an absence of evidence, and
to delineate when it will allow inferences to be drawn from inconclusive social
science evidence.

[Sujit Choudhry, at
p. 530]

89

In the case of
R. v. Jones
,
1986 CanLII 32 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R.
284, La Forest J. stated that “[a] court must be taken to have a
general knowledge of our history and values and to know at least the broad
design and workings of our society” (at p. 299).  And (
ibid.
):

No proof is required to show the importance of
education in our society or its significance to government.  ….  Nor is
evidence necessary to establish the difficulty of administering a general
provincial educational scheme if the onus lies on the educational authorities
to enforce compliance.

See also,
Edwards
Books and Art Ltd.
, at p. 802.

90

More recently, in the case of
Sauv
é
v.
Canada (Chief Electoral Officer
),
2002 SCC 68
, [2002]
3 S.C.R. 519, McLachlin C.J.C. stated the following (at para. 18):

… [L]
egislative
justification does not require empirical proof in a scientific sense.  While
some matters can be proved with empirical or mathematical precision, others,
involving philosophical, political and social considerations, cannot.  In this
case, it is enough that the justification be convincing, in the sense that it
is sufficient to satisfy the reasonable person looking at all the evidence and
relevant considerations, that the state is justified in infringing the right at
stake to the degree it has:  ….  What is required is “rational, reasoned
defensibility”:  ….  Common sense and inferential reasoning may supplement the
evidence:  ….

91

And most recently, the Supreme Court of Canada
discussed this point in the case of
Bryan
.  The issue in that case was
whether a law that prohibited the broadcasting of election results until
polling stations closed in all parts of Canada infringed the appellant’s
s.
2(b)

Charter
rights and, if so, whether the infringement was justified
under
s. 1
.  Bastarache J. stated (at para. 22):

In some cases, the objective asserted by the
government will be largely a matter of the “values and principles essential to
a free and democratic society”.

In such cases, it may not
be appropriate to require proof according to the usual civil requirements.
This approach is also espoused by Professor Hogg in
Constitutional Law of
Canada
(at para. 38.4):

For these reasons, in my opinion, it would be
desirable for
Charter
review to become less dependent on evidence, even if the
courts have to strain somewhat to make “obvious” or “self-evident” findings.

92

So, in which cases would the justification be
self-evident?  It is often argued that whether or not something is
“self-evident” appears to be quite subjective.  As McLachlin C.J.C. warned in
Sauv
é
, at
para.
18
, and Abella J. referred to recently in
Bryan
, at para.
103
,
“one must be wary of stereotypes cloaked as common sense, and of substituting
deference for the reasoned demonstration required by s. 1.”

93

In this case, the provisions of the
Code

itself are neutral.  The lawyer must act with integrity and in a professional
manner.  Histed’s real objection lies in the application of the neutral
provisions of the
Code
to the facts of this case; in other words, to the
decision of the panel.  It was the panel’s decision that the word “bigot” on
these facts contravened the provisions of the
Code
and were grounds for
discipline.  There is no appeal as to the reasonableness of this decision in an
administrative law sense.  However, the Law Society must still establish that
the decision was justifiable under s. 1.  As the Supreme Court explained in
Ross
,
a case also involving a constitutional challenge to a Board’s order, an
administrative tribunal acting pursuant to its delegated powers exceeds its
jurisdiction if it makes an order that infringes the
Charter
.  The
Charter

standard and the administrative law standard must not be combined into one.
When the values invoked are
Charter
values, it is necessary to subject
the decision to a
s. 1
analysis.

94

In this situation, it is difficult to imagine what
reasonable evidence might have been presented by the Law Society in front of
the discipline panel to establish specifically that it was necessary to discipline
a lawyer for calling a judge a bigot in order to maintain respect for the
administration of justice and to adequately protect the public, while calling a
judge right-wing or slow would not cross that line.  It should be remembered
that no attempt was made in this case to establish the truth of the allegation
that the judge was indeed a bigot.  While Histed emphasized several times at
the panel hearing that he was simply stating a truth, he led no evidence on
that point.  The panel held that the opportunity for proof rested with the
party making the allegation and Histed had had his opportunity and did not take
advantage of it.

95

Not only is it unlikely that determinative evidence
would be available on these points (even on a standard of reasonable apprehension
of harm), the practical implications of calling such evidence in every
discipline hearing would result in chaos.  Even if such evidence was available,
is it reasonable to expect that the Law Society could requisition and adduce
empirical or social science evidence to every discipline hearing?  It is clear
that legislation that infringes
Charter
rights must be clearly
justified.  However, where the legislation is found to be justified, an
attenuated level of s. 1 justification should be sufficient to justify an
otherwise administratively reasonable decision.  This is particularly the case
where the legislation and the proceeding are based upon reference points which,
while not vague, are highly normative.  Surely, an ambit of operation must be
left in the hands of the quasi-judicial tribunal who has the expertise and has
been vested with the task by the legislature.  Perhaps this is the type of case
where the justification is self-evident.

96

Fortunately, given the controversial nature of this
issue, I do not have to decide it in this case.  I believe there is some
evidence on which I can rely, which evidence, given the nature of the
infringement, is sufficient to satisfy the onus.

97

A review of the decision discloses that the panel
considered and relied on a number of pieces of evidence.  First, there is the
legislation itself, which, in s. 3(1) of the
Act
, mandates the Law
Society to uphold and protect the public interest in the delivery of legal
services with competence, integrity and independence.  Second, there are the
provisions of the
Code
which, when read together, provide guidance and
an intelligible standard as to what is or is not permissible in communications
with other counsel (especially Chapter 15).

98

The panel also relied on jurisprudence on point
both from courts and other disciplinary bodies.  Reliance on other case law can
satisfy the s. 1 evidentiary onus.  For example, in the case of
Bryan
,
in upholding the black-out on the publication of election results, the Supreme
Court relied on the fact that maintaining confidence in the electoral process
had been determined to be a clearly pressing and substantial objective in its
earlier decision in
Harper v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
2004 SCC 33
,
[2004] 1 S.C.R. 827.  Bastarache J. stated (at para. 34):

… [S]ome objectives, once asserted, can be simply
accepted by the Court as
always
pressing and substantial in any society
that purports to operate in accordance with the tenets of a free and democratic
society.

99

Some cases, with respect to the objectives stated,
have already been discussed.  The panel also referred to other decisions where
remarks made about specific judges were found to be unprofessional and gave
rise to findings of professional misconduct, such as
Kessiloff v. Law
Society of Manitoba
,
1983 CanLII 3674 (MB CA)
, [1983] 3 W.W.R. 190 (Man. C.A.),
Kopyto
,
Law
Society of British Columbia v. Glenford Emerson Greene
, [2003] LSBC 30, and

Law Society of British Columbia v. Karl Eisbrenner
, [2003] LSBC 03.

100

For example, in the
Eisbrenner
case, the
panel held that while a member of an independent bar must retain some right to
fairly comment on the performance of the judiciary, comments intended to convey
the impression that the judge was incompetent and biased transcended the limits
of fair criticism.  See para. 47.  In the
Greene
decision, Greene was
disciplined for referring to two judges as “two of the dumbest Judges this side
of an asylum,” the panel commenting (at para. 34):

It is not in the best interests of the justice system,
our clients, and ourselves to express ourselves in a fashion which promotes
acrimony or intensifies the stressfulness or the difficulty of those already
stressful and difficult circumstances.

101

In justifying infringements of freedom of
expression under s. 1, the Supreme Court has consistently held that the level
of constitutional protection varies with the nature of that expression.  The
protection afforded freedom of expression will diminish where conduct that is
initially protected moves farther away from the core values protected by s. 2(b),
such as the search for political, artistic and scientific truth, the protection
of individual autonomy and self-development and the promotion of public
participation in the democratic process.  See
Canadian Broadcasting Corp. v.
New Brunswick (Attorney General)
,
1996 CanLII 184 (SCC)
, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 480 at para.
63
, and
RJR-MacDonald
,
at para. 72.

102

As Wilson J. noted in
Edmonton Journal v.
Alberta (Attorney General)
,
1989 CanLII 20 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1326, not all expression is
equally worthy of protection.  Nor are all infringements of free expression
equally serious.  This was again repeated in the
Ross
case dealing with
a teacher’s right to express anti-Semitic comments outside of the classroom.
The Supreme Court pointed out that such expression was, at best, tenuously
connected to the core values of freedom of expression, and consequently, an
attenuated level of s. 1 justification was appropriate.

103

So, for example, in
R. v. Lucas
,
1998 CanLII 815 (SCC)
, [1998] 1
S.C.R. 439, where, in finding that the
Criminal Code
prohibition on
defamatory libel was a justifiable infringement of s. 2(b), Cory J. said (at
paras. 88-89):

….  When freedom of expression is at issue, it is
logical that the nature of the violation should be taken into consideration in
the delicate balancing process.  ….

In
Stevens
, [
(1995),
1995 CanLII 5594 (MB CA)
,
100 Man.R. (2d) 81
(C.A.)
], at [para. 163], Twaddle J.A. aptly noted that based on the decision of
La Forest J. in
United States of America v. Cotroni
,
1989 CanLII 106 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R.
1469
:

The more worthy [the] activity, the more difficult it
is to justify a limit on it.  On the other hand, a limit on activity which is
harmful to another and far removed from the values embodied in the freedom of
expression can more readily be justified.

104

In the case at hand, the prohibition in the
Code

is against offensive and unprofessional expression and the panel held that it
was the use of the word “bigot” that was unprofessional, not criticism of the
judge.  It is the form of expression being infringed, not the expression
itself.  Surely, restrictions on forms of expression that consist essentially
of gratuitous insults in a forum of professional dealings will require little
by way of external justification.

105

As well, in coming to its conclusion that the use
of the word “bigot” was unprofessional within the meaning of the
Code
,
the panel relied on dictionary definitions of the term.  The word “bigot” is
defined in
Webster’s Third International Dictionary
as:

obstinately and blindly attached to some creed,
opinion or practice often intolerantly devoted to his own church, party, belief
or opinion.

The
Compact Edition
Oxford Dictionary
defines “bigot” as:

hypocrite; a person obstinately and unreasonably
wedded to a particular creed, opinion or ritual,

and “bigotry” as:

intolerant towards others.

106

Even more so, the panel had Histed’s
acknowledgement that:

(1)

the word “bigot” meant “importing racism, stupidity
and the lack of an open mind”;

(2)

a bigot should never be appointed to the bench, and
if discovered after appointment, should be removed; and

(3)

the judge was incapable of hearing the matter
fairly and impartially and did not have sufficient intelligence to discharge
his obligation as a judge.

107

Given those undisputed meanings attached to the
word “bigot” and the fundamental role that impartiality plays in the role of a
judge, the link between the objective and the means used becomes self-evident.
I do not believe that more evidence than that mentioned above is required to
establish that such comments from a lawyer which go to the core of the judicial
function bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

108

Moreover, the impairment is minimal affecting not
the fact of criticism, but only the form of criticism and resulting not in a
criminal contempt charge (see
Kopyto
), but rather a fine in professional
disciplinary hearings.  The penalty is imposed only after a fair hearing
conducted by an impartial tribunal.  An appropriate balance is struck between
freedom of expression and the need to maintain some sense of decorum and
professionalism in the way in which legal proceedings are conducted in this
country.

CONCLUSION

109

I would dismiss this appeal.  In its decision, the
panel correctly dealt with the issues of privilege and the admissibility of
evidence.
The Privacy Act
does not apply to the letter in question, nor
does the concept of settlement privilege.  Even if settlement privilege did
apply, on the facts of this case, the public interest in the effective
regulation of lawyers by an independent bar would require that the governing
body have access to the letter.

110

The panel also correctly dealt with the impact of
the
Charter
on rules enacted by the Law Society to properly govern its
members in the public interest.  The provisions of the
Code
constitute a
balanced approach to dealing with pressing and substantial objectives; namely,
the need to regulate the conduct of the profession so as to protect the public
and the need to maintain respect for the administration of justice.

111

The panel gave due consideration to the importance
of freedom of expression.  They did so in conjunction with a consideration of
the pressing and substantial need to maintain the respect for the
administration of justice by disciplining members of its profession for
expressing opinions in a manner which is disrespectful, unprofessional and
offensive.  At the conclusion of its balanced consideration, the panel properly
concluded that even if in regulating Histed’s conduct as a member of the Law
Society, it was restricting his right to express himself (by calling a judge a
bigot in a letter to opposing counsel), such a restriction was a reasonable
limit under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

112

The appeals are dismissed with costs.
